summary: Extends the Management Information Base with objects for managing the Fabric Element portion of the Fibre Channel standards. It lets network management tools monitor Fibre Channel switches. It is on the standards track and was replaced by RFC 4044.

eli5.summary: A switch in a storage network needs a dashboard. This lists the numbers and settings a manager can read from it from far away.

questions: how to monitor fibre channel switch
subtitle: SNMP monitoring objects for Fibre Channel storage network switches.

tldr.problem: Storage networks using Fibre Channel require remote monitoring and management. Network administrators need to check the status of switch ports, monitor error rates, track throughput, and manage switch configuration from a central system.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC defines a set of Management Information Base (MIB) objects that can be accessed via SNMP. It organizes objects into groups for configuration (modules and ports), operational status, error counters, accounting statistics, and capabilities, allowing administrators to monitor and manage Fibre Channel fabric elements remotely.
tldr.outcome: Administrators can monitor switch health, detect link failures, track performance, and configure ports from a central management station. It was superseded by RFC 4044.

today: This RFC was obsoleted by RFC 4044, which consolidated and updated Fibre Channel management definitions. However, the core MIB organization and monitoring concepts remain relevant for network administrators managing storage area networks.

sections.title: Fibre Channel Fabric Structure
sections.content:
A Fibre Channel Fabric is a network of switches that carries storage traffic. The smallest unit is a Fabric Element (a switch), which has ports. Ports are grouped into logical or physical modules for management. F_Ports connect to single storage devices (N_Ports); FL_Ports connect to loops with up to 126 devices (NL_Ports). An administrator managing a Fibre Channel network needs visibility into the health and performance of each switch module and port.

This RFC defines management objects for a Fabric Element, its modules, and its ports. The management model divides information into groups: Configuration (module and port settings), Status (current operational state), Error (counter data for diagnostics), Accounting (performance statistics), and Capabilities (what the switch supports).
sections.eli5: A Fibre Channel switch is a little city of post office doors. Some doors lead to individual buildings (N_Ports), some lead to little circles of buildings (NL_Ports). The switch is organized into neighborhoods (modules). An administrator needs a map of the city and a way to count how busy each door is.

sections.title: Configuration Group
sections.content:
The Configuration group contains scalar objects describing the entire Fabric Element and table entries for each module and port. fcFeModuleCapacity is the maximum number of modules the switch can contain (constant across reboots). fcFeModuleTable has one entry per installed module; each entry includes the module index, description, operational status (online, offline, testing, faulty), and the maximum number of ports that module can hold. fcFeFxPortConfigTable (the FxPort Configuration Table) contains one entry per port with configuration settings such as buffer-to-buffer credit (how many frames can be in flight), receive data field size (frame payload size), and operational parameters.

Modules and ports can be sparsely numbered; a 13-card cage might have cards 3, 5, 6 and 7 installed. Module numbers and port numbers do not have to be contiguous. This allows a vendor to map module numbers to physical slot numbers without renumbering when a card is removed and replaced.
sections.eli5: The Configuration group is like a building directory. It says how many mailboxes the building can hold, which mailboxes are in which hallways, and whether each mailbox is working or broken. It also says how many letters each mailbox can hold waiting to be picked up.

sections.title: Status and Error Monitoring
sections.content:
The Status group contains the current operational state of each port. For each FxPort, objects report the current speed (1 Gbps, 2 Gbps, etc.), the link state (up or down), the attached NxPort's name and address (if any), and negotiated parameters like buffer credit and frame size. The Status group also includes physical-level information such as received signal strength and synchronization status.

The Error group tracks various kinds of errors detected by each port: CRC errors (data corruption during transmission), disparity errors (signal encoding errors), primitive sequence errors (frame timing errors), address errors, and more. These counters help diagnose link quality and are useful for predicting failures before a link goes down completely. A high error rate on a link might indicate a failing transceiver or a marginal cable.
sections.eli5: The Status group is like a real-time display showing which mailbox doors are open or closed, and what is on the other side. The Error group is like a logbook counting every time a letter arrived torn, or a mailbox door jammed. High error counts mean something is wearing out.

sections.title: Accounting and Capability Groups
sections.content:
The Accounting group contains per-port statistics for performance analysis. Separate tables track Class 1 (connection-oriented, reserved bandwidth), Class 2 (datagram with delivery confirmation), and Class 3 (unreliable datagram) traffic. For each class, the switch records frame counts (how many frames sent and received), byte counts, and various frame types (data frames, link control frames, etc.). These statistics let an administrator calculate throughput, identify the busiest links, and spot traffic imbalances.

The Capability group declares what services each port and module supports: Class of Service capabilities (which traffic classes are supported), buffer-to-buffer credit model (regular or alternate), maximum frame size supported, and other inherent characteristics. These are read-only objects that describe the switch's fixed hardware and firmware capabilities.
sections.eli5: The Accounting group is like a logbook saying "yesterday 10,000 letters went through mailbox A, and 2,000 through mailbox B." The Capability group is like a label on each mailbox saying "this box can hold large packages" or "this box does not accept international mail."

sections.title: MIB Organization and Implementation
sections.content:
The MIB module is named FIBRE-CHANNEL-FE-MIB and is rooted under the standard Internet MIB tree at { mib-2 75 }. It uses SMIv2 syntax, making it machine-readable and automatically translatable to older SMIv1 format for legacy management stations. The module defines textual conventions (custom data types) for Fibre Channel-specific values: FcNameId (an 8-byte Fibre Channel world-wide name), FcAddressId (a 24-bit address), FcRxDataFieldSize (frame payload size limits), and FcCosCap (class-of-service capabilities as a bit field).

A Fabric Element MUST support reading these objects via SNMP GET and SNMP GETNEXT commands. Some objects are read-write (allowing remote configuration), while others are read-only (hardware facts). The module also defines compliance groups and conformance information for testing whether an implementation meets the standard.
sections.eli5: The MIB is like a standardized form filed away in a cabinet. Every switch that claims to support this MIB must fill out the same form with the same questions in the same order, so a manager can read any switch's form without retraining.
